The database holds intersection details including an identifier, district, and layout type, along with signal timings containing the time of day, green duration, and red duration. First, create a view isolating morning timing records where the green duration is under thirty seconds and the red duration exceeds one minute. Next, create a second view that links these restrictive timings to their intersections and counts the number of such timings per district. Finally, write a query that retrieves districts having more than five restrictive intersections, displaying the district and the count, ordered by the count from highest to lowest. Example input: a morning timing with twenty seconds green and seventy seconds red. Example output: the north district and a count of twelve.

title: Dry cleaning solvent recycling
spec: Write an SQL script with an entry procedure `evaluate(cycles)` to analyze solvent recovery in dry cleaning machines. You are provided with machine profiles containing an identifier, model, and capacity, as well as operational cycles recording the date, gallons of solvent used, and gallons recovered. First, build a view that isolates cycle records from the past month where more than five gallons of solvent were used. Then, construct a second view linking these cycles to the machine profiles to calculate the average recovery percentage for each model. Finally, write the main query to select machine models whose average recovery is below eighty percent, outputting the model and the average percentage, sorted by the lowest recovery rate first. Example input: a cycle using ten gallons and recovering seven. Example output: the eco master model with a seventy percent recovery rate.

title: Historical windmill sail repair
spec: Write an SQL script featuring a procedure `inspect(sails)` to track wind damage on traditional windmills. The data includes windmill locations with an identifier, region, and year built, alongside maintenance logs detailing the repair date, damage type, and total cost. First, create a view that filters the maintenance logs for repairs occurring in the last year specifically caused by wind tearing where the cost exceeds five hundred dollars. Next, create a view that joins these expensive repairs with the windmill locations to sum the total repair costs per region. Finally, write a query to display the regions and their total repair costs, ordering the list from highest to lowest cost. Example input: a wind tear repair costing six hundred dollars in the valley. Example output: the valley region and a total cost of four thousand dollars.

title: Water slide friction coefficient
spec: Write an SQL script with a main routine `analyze(tests)` to review safety measurements on water slides. The system tracks slide properties including the name, park location, and vertical drop, as well as test measurements showing the test date, rider weight class, and recorded friction value. First, define a view that captures recent tests involving heavy riders where the friction value is recorded above zero point four. Next, establish a second view that connects these high friction tests to the slide properties and calculates the average friction value for each slide. Finally, write a query that lists slides in the central park location exceeding this average threshold, displaying the slide name and average friction, sorted by the highest friction. Example input: a heavy rider test with a friction of zero point five. Example output: the doom drop slide with an average friction of zero point four eight.

title: Ferris wheel passenger balancing
spec: Write an SQL script containing a procedure `balance(loads)` to monitor weight distribution on a giant observation wheel. Available records include cabin specifications indicating the cabin number and maximum capacity, and boarding events recording the ride timestamp, passenger count, and total weight. First, generate a view that filters boarding events for evening rides where the passenger count is at least four and the weight exceeds three hundred kilograms. Second, create a view that joins these heavy boarding events to their respective cabins to calculate the total weight carried per ride timestamp. Finally, write a query extracting ride timestamps where the aggregate weight across all cabins surpasses five thousand kilograms, ordered chronologically. Example input: a cabin loaded with six passengers weighing four hundred kilograms. Example output: an evening ride timestamp and a total weight of five thousand two hundred kilograms.

title: Professional diving board spring tension
spec: Write an SQL script with an entry function `calibrate(boards)` to assess the stiffness of aquatic diving boards. The data comprises facility records detailing the facility name and city, board inventories with an identifier and stiffness rating, and mechanical tests logging the test date, applied force, and downward deflection distance. First, create a view that isolates mechanical tests performed with maximum force where the deflection distance is under twenty centimeters. Next, create a view linking these stiff test results to the boards and facilities to compute the average deflection distance per facility. Finally, select and output the facilities and their average deflection, restricting results to cities in the northern region, and order them alphabetically by city name. Example input: a maximum force test yielding eighteen centimeters of deflection. Example output: the downtown aquatic center with an average deflection of nineteen centimeters.

title: Mini golf course turf replacement
spec: Write an SQL script headed by a procedure `schedule(greens)` to analyze maintenance expenses across miniature golf venues. Information is stored as course profiles containing the theme and location, individual holes with their wear level, and financial replacements tracking the replacement date and material cost. First, draft a view that filters for holes classified with severe wear that were replaced during the spring season. Then, design a view joining these spring replacements to their parent courses to calculate the total replacement cost per course theme. Finally, formulate a query that identifies course themes with total spring replacement costs exceeding one thousand dollars, ordered by the total cost in descending order. Example input: a severe wear hole replaced for two hundred dollars. Example output: the pirate adventure theme with a total cost of one thousand five hundred dollars.

title: Go kart tire tread depth
spec: Write an SQL script utilizing a main procedure `monitor(karts)` to flag unsafe racing vehicles. The system contains a registry of go karts specifying their identifier and assigned track, and inspection logs detailing the date and tread depth for all four tires. First, construct a view that filters inspections from the summer season where any single tire shows a tread depth below two millimeters. Next, build a view that joins these failed inspections to the kart registry to count the number of unsafe inspections per track. Finally, extract the tracks that have recorded more than ten unsafe kart inspections, outputting the track name and the failure count, sorted by the highest count. Example input: an inspection showing a front left tread of one millimeter. Example output: the grand prix track with twelve failed inspections.

title: Zipline cable tensioning logs
spec: Write an SQL script with a primary routine `review(cables)` to ensure the structural integrity of aerial adventure routes. Provided data includes route specifications mapping the route name to its overall length, and daily tension logs capturing the date, ambient temperature, and tension reading. First, create a view filtering for tension logs recorded on days when the temperature was below freezing and the tension fell below safe operational limits. Next, create a view joining these low tension logs with the route specifications to determine the lowest recorded tension for each route. Finally, write a query that lists routes longer than two hundred meters that experienced these dangerous drops, ordered by the route name. Example input: a tension log showing low tension on a freezing day. Example output: the canopy glide route with a minimum tension of four hundred units.

title: Stilts walking balance stability
spec: Write an SQL script incorporating a procedure `evaluate(performances)` to analyze safety incidents for circus performers. The database holds performer profiles indicating their experience level, stilt pairs detailing the construction material, and practice sessions logging the duration and number of falls. First, make a view that isolates practice sessions lasting longer than an hour where the performer fell more than three times. Then, create a view that links these high fall sessions to novice performers and groups them by stilt material to calculate the average number of falls. Finally, output the stilt materials that average more than four falls for novices, ordered by the highest average fall count. Example input: a novice performer falling five times on wooden stilts. Example output: aluminum stilts with an average of four point five falls.

title: Trapeze bar grip tape longevity
spec: Write an SQL script led by a routine `assess(bars)` to track equipment wear in acrobatics studios. Records consist of studio locations categorized by region, trapeze bars identifying the applied tape brand, and usage logs documenting the hours flown and the percentage of tape peeling. First, write a view capturing usage logs where the tape exhibits over fifty percent peeling in under twenty hours of flight time. Next, develop a view that joins these rapid degradation logs with the studio data to count the number of premature failures per tape brand in each region. Finally, query the results to show tape brands with over twenty failures in the western region, sorted alphabetically by brand. Example input: a log showing sixty percent peeling after ten hours. Example output: the sticky grip brand with twenty five failures in the western region.

title: Tightrope wire sag measurement
spec: Write an SQL script containing an entry function `measure(wires)` to evaluate tension loss in highwire acts. The input includes venue properties indicating if they are indoor or outdoor, wire details specifying the length, and calibration tests recording the center weight applied and the resulting sag depth. First, establish a view that filters calibration tests using a heavy center weight where the sag depth exceeds fifteen centimeters. Then, construct a view connecting these excessive sag tests to outdoor venues and their specific wires to calculate the maximum sag per wire. Finally, query this aggregated data to output wires longer than ten meters that failed the sag test, ordered by their maximum sag depth. Example input: a test showing eighteen centimeters of sag under a heavy load. Example output: a twelve meter wire with a maximum sag of nineteen centimeters.

title: Bull riding mechanical bucking patterns
spec: Write an SQL script with a main procedure `analyze(rides)` to evaluate the performance of mechanical training bulls. Data is stored as machine records listing the model and manufacturer, and ride sessions logging the difficulty setting, average spin rate, and average buck height. First, formulate a view that isolates ride sessions set to the highest difficulty where the average buck height exceeded one meter. Next, create a view that links these intense sessions to the machine records to calculate the average spin rate per manufacturer. Finally, write a query that returns manufacturers whose intense sessions maintain an average spin rate above forty revolutions per minute, sorted by spin rate descending. Example input: a maximum difficulty session with a one point two meter buck height. Example output: the rodeo master manufacturer with an average spin rate of forty five.

title: Wave pool pump pressure
spec: Write an SQL script featuring a primary routine `monitor(pumps)` to detect mechanical faults in artificial wave pools. The available data covers simulator zones with their location, pump units detailing their horsepower, and telemetry readings capturing the timestamp, pressure output, and flow rate. First, define a view that filters telemetry readings where the pressure output drops below fifty units while the flow rate remains high. Second, create a view joining these anomalous readings to high horsepower pumps to count the number of low pressure events per simulator location. Finally, extract locations that experienced more than fifteen low pressure events in a single week, ordered by the event count from highest to lowest. Example input: a reading showing forty pressure units with a high flow rate. Example output: the north beach simulator with twenty low pressure events.

title: Laser tag vest hit sensors
spec: Write an SQL script with a main function `troubleshoot(vests)` to identify faulty entertainment equipment. The system maintains arena details including the capacity, vest inventories with their purchase date, and match diagnostics recording the hits taken and sensor error codes generated. First, build a view that filters match diagnostics for games where a vest generated more than five sensor error codes despite recording few hits. Then, construct a view joining these faulty matches to vests purchased in the last calendar year to sum the errors per arena. Finally, query the summarized data to display arenas that accumulated over one hundred sensor errors from new vests, sorted alphabetically by arena name. Example input: a match where a new vest generated seven error codes. Example output: the galactic zone arena with one hundred and twenty errors.

title: Airsoft pellet velocity chronographs
spec: Write an SQL script led by a procedure `verify(markers)` to enforce safety limits in recreational shooting leagues. Input data involves team profiles listing their competitive division, marker assignments detailing the equipment model, and chronograph shots recording the pellet weight and feet per second velocity. First, draft a view that isolates shots using heavy weight pellets that register a velocity over four hundred feet per second. Next, design a view that links these over limit shots to their respective teams and models to calculate the average excessive velocity for the professional division. Finally, output the equipment models that average over four hundred and twenty feet per second, ordered by the highest velocity. Example input: a heavy pellet shot traveling at four hundred and ten feet per second. Example output: the striker model with an average velocity of four hundred and twenty five.

title: Slot car track power fluctuations
spec: Write an SQL script containing a routine `track(lanes)` to diagnose electrical issues in miniature racing circuits. Data is provided as track profiles detailing the overall length, lane assignments specifying the color, and power logs capturing the timestamp, voltage, and amperage. First, create a view that filters power logs for moments when the voltage drops below ten volts while the amperage surges above safe levels. Then, build a view connecting these power drops to the red lanes across all tracks to determine the total duration of voltage drops per track. Finally, write a query listing tracks longer than fifty feet that suffered more than five minutes of voltage drops, sorted by track length. Example input: a log showing nine volts and high amperage on the red lane. Example output: the grand circuit track with seven minutes of voltage drops.

title: Remote control airplane servo angles
spec: Write an SQL script with an entry function `calibrate(servos)` to optimize flight profiles for remote control aircraft. The database includes model specifications noting the weight class, and flight telemetry logging the maximum servo angle and the overall stability score. First, form a view that captures flight telemetry where the maximum angle exceeded twelve degrees and the stability score remained above ninety. Next, create a view linking these successful aggressive flights to their model specifications to compute the average stability score per weight class. Finally, query this aggregated information to return weight classes that maintain an average stability score above ninety five, ordered by the score descending. Example input: a flight with thirteen degrees of angle and a stability score of ninety two. Example output: the heavy lifter class with an average stability score of ninety six.

title: Robot vacuum mapping collisions
spec: Write an SQL script employing a procedure `map(cleanings)` to evaluate navigation software in automated cleaning devices. Available records comprise vacuum profiles noting the firmware version, and run logs detailing the room size, cleaning duration, and number of obstacle collisions. First, write a view that filters run logs for small rooms under fifteen square meters where the vacuum registered more than twenty collisions. Then, create a view joining these high collision runs to the vacuum profiles to calculate the average number of collisions per firmware version. Finally, extract firmware versions released this year that average more than twenty five collisions in small rooms, sorted by the collision count from highest to lowest. Example input: a run in a ten square meter room with twenty two collisions. Example output: firmware version seven with an average of twenty eight collisions.

title: Lawn mower blade sharpening intervals
spec: Write an SQL script featuring a main routine `schedule(mowers)` to optimize landscaping equipment maintenance. Data consists of crew assignments detailing their operating region, mower registries noting the brand, and usage records tracking the hours operated and the type of grass cut. First, generate a view that isolates usage records where equipment cut thick grass for extended continuous hours. Next, construct a view connecting these heavy usage records to the mower brands and crew regions to sum the total hours operated without sharpening. Finally, query the summarized data to find brands in the southern region that exceed fifty hours of unsharpened operation on thick grass, ordered by total hours. Example input: a mower used on thick grass for eight continuous hours. Example output: the green cut brand with sixty total hours of operation.

title: Chainsaw chain link lubrication
spec: Write an SQL script with a procedure `inspect(chainsaws)` to monitor oil consumption in forestry operations. The information includes forest zones specifying the timber density, chainsaw profiles noting the guide bar length, and maintenance entries logging the cutting hours and liters of oil consumed. First, draft a view that filters maintenance entries for chainsaws operating continuously where oil consumption exceeds two liters per hour. Then, develop a view joining these high consumption entries to chainsaws with long guide bars and their respective forest zones to calculate the average oil consumption rate per zone. Finally, output the forest zones with dense timber that average over two point five liters per hour, sorted alphabetically by zone name. Example input: an entry showing three liters of oil used in one hour. Example output: the pine ridge zone with an average consumption of two point six liters.

title: Snow blower auger sheer pins
spec: Write an SQL script headed by a main function `review(blowers)` to track mechanical failures during winter storms. The database holds municipal records noting the average annual snowfall, blower inventories detailing the engine size, and repair tickets logging the snow wetness level and the number of broken sheer pins. First, establish a view that filters repair tickets for heavy wet snow conditions where more than three sheer pins were broken in a single shift. Next, construct a view linking these frequent breakdowns to large engine blowers to count the total number of broken pins per municipality. Finally, query the results to list municipalities with heavy snowfall that recorded over fifty broken sheer pins, ordered by the failure count descending. Example input: a repair ticket for four broken pins in wet snow. Example output: the northville municipality with sixty broken sheer pins.

title: Leaf blower air velocity profiling
spec: Write an SQL script containing a procedure `analyze(blowers)` to evaluate the performance of groundskeeping tools. Input involves department registries listing the campus location, unit specifications detailing the power source, and performance tests recording the measurement distance and generated wind speed. First, write a view isolating performance tests measured at a distance of five feet where the wind speed dropped below one hundred miles per hour. Then, create a view joining these underperforming tests to battery powered units to determine the average wind speed for each campus location. Finally, extract campuses where the average wind speed of battery units is below ninety miles per hour at that distance, sorted by campus name. Example input: a test at five feet recording ninety five miles per hour. Example output: the west side campus with an average wind speed of eighty eight miles per hour.

title: Pressure washer nozzle wear
spec: Write an SQL script with an entry routine `evaluate(nozzles)` to analyze degradation in exterior cleaning equipment. Available records include operator profiles detailing their cleaning specialty, washer units noting the maximum pressure rating, and usage logs documenting the nozzle type, hours used, and spray pattern degradation level. First, draft a view that filters usage logs for turbo nozzles that show severe spray pattern degradation after less than thirty hours of use. Next, create a view connecting these rapid wear logs to high pressure washers to count the number of failed nozzles per cleaning specialty. Finally, write a query that returns specialties that experienced more than ten rapid turbo nozzle failures, ordered by the failure count from highest to lowest. Example input: a turbo nozzle showing severe degradation after twenty hours. Example output: the industrial cleaning specialty with fifteen failed nozzles.

title: Professional dog surfing competition
spec: Write a SQL function `analyze(minimum)` that takes a numeric minimum wave height. The database has a table for dogs with columns for the dog identifier, breed, and owner name. Another table records surfing rides with the dog identifier, wave height in feet, ride duration in seconds, and a boolean for whether they wiped out. First, find all rides where the dog did not wipe out and the wave height is strictly greater than the given minimum. Join these rides with the dogs table to group the results by breed. Calculate the total number of successful rides and the average ride duration for each breed. Finally, return the breed, total rides, and average duration, but only include breeds that have more than five successful rides, sorting the final list from highest average duration to lowest. Example input: a minimum height of four feet, with golden retrievers having six successful rides averaging twenty seconds. Example output: a single row containing the golden retriever breed, six for the count, and twenty for the average.

title: Extreme ironing altitude records
spec: Write a database routine `summarize(elevation)` that accepts a numeric altitude threshold. The schema contains an ironers table tracking the ironer identifier, name, and nationality. A separate sessions table logs extreme ironing attempts with the ironer identifier, mountain peak name, altitude in meters, garments pressed, and wind speed. Filter the sessions to include only those where the wind speed is below twenty and the altitude is above the provided elevation. Match these valid sessions to their respective ironers and group the data by nationality. Sum the total number of garments pressed for each nationality, filtering out any nationalities that pressed ten or fewer garments overall. Return the nationality and the summed garments, ordering the results from the highest number of garments to the lowest. For example, if French ironers pressed twelve garments at valid altitudes, the output row shows the French nationality and twelve.

title: Parrot vocabulary acquisition
spec: Create a query function `evaluate(limit)` that takes a maximum number of days as a numeric parameter. You are provided a parrots table containing the parrot identifier, species, and age. A second words table logs vocabulary progress with the parrot identifier, the word learned, syllable count, and days taken to learn. Narrow down the words to those with two or more syllables where the days taken is strictly less than the given limit. Connect these fast-learned words to the parrots table to group the records by species. Compute the average days taken to learn these complex words for each species, keeping only species that have learned at least four qualifying words. Output the species and their average learning days, sorted from the fastest average time to the slowest. Example: if macaws learned five words in an average of three days, the result lists the macaw species and the number three.

title: Giant pumpkin weighing contest
spec: Construct a reporting function `rank(target)` that accepts a numeric minimum weight. You have a growers table recording the grower identifier, home region, and years of experience. A pumpkins table logs the grower identifier, circumference, weight in pounds, and fertilizer type used. Filter the records to find pumpkins grown with organic fertilizer that weigh strictly more than the target weight. Link these records to the growers to group the data by the home region. Calculate the maximum weight and the average circumference for each region, keeping only those regions where the average circumference exceeds one hundred. Return the region and the maximum weight, ordering the final rows by the maximum weight in descending order. Example input: a target weight of five hundred pounds, yielding an output where the western region shows a maximum weight of six hundred.

title: Koala eucalyptus leaf consumption
spec: Write a database procedure `tabulate(hours)` that takes a maximum digestion time as a numeric input. There is a koalas table with the koala identifier, forest zone, and health status. A meals table tracks the koala identifier, leaf type, weight consumed in grams, and digestion hours. Filter for meals consisting of blue gum leaves where the digestion time is less than the provided hours parameter. Join these meals with the koalas table so you can group the results by the forest zone. Sum the total weight of leaves consumed in each zone, restricting the output to zones that had at least three distinct meals recorded. Output the forest zone and the total weight consumed, sorted from the highest total weight to the lowest. Example: given an hours limit of four, the northern zone might return with a total consumption of eight hundred grams.

title: Pufferfish inflation durations
spec: Develop a SQL routine `report(size)` that accepts a minimum inflation diameter. The system holds a puffers table containing the pufferfish identifier, ocean sector, and color pattern. A deflations table tracks the pufferfish identifier, predator type, inflation diameter in centimeters, and duration in seconds. Isolate the defensive events triggered by sharks where the inflation diameter is strictly greater than the given size. Merge these events with the puffers table and group the records by color pattern. Calculate the average inflation duration for each pattern, ensuring you only keep patterns with an average duration greater than twenty seconds. Return the color pattern and the average duration, ordering the list from the longest average duration to the shortest. Example: a striped pattern facing sharks might output an average duration of thirty seconds.

title: Competitive cheese rolling injuries
spec: Create a query script `calculate(tumbles)` that takes a numeric maximum for falls. The database includes a runners table with the runner identifier, age bracket, and shoe type. A races table records the runner identifier, hill gradient percentage, tumbles taken, and finish time in seconds. Restrict the races to those held on gradients steeper than twenty percent where the runner took fewer tumbles than the specified maximum. Combine this with the runners table to group the outcomes by shoe type. Compute the average finish time for each shoe type, retaining only shoe types used by at least five qualifying runners. Output the shoe type and the average finish time, sorted sequentially from the fastest average time to the slowest. For instance, cleated shoes might appear in the output with an average finish time of forty seconds.

title: Homing pigeon navigation errors
spec: Write a data function `assess(wind)` that receives a numeric minimum headwind speed. The schema stores a pigeons table with the pigeon identifier, flock name, and wingspan. A flights table captures the pigeon identifier, distance in miles, deviation in degrees, and headwind speed. Filter the data to find flights covering more than fifty miles where the headwind speed exceeded the given minimum. Join the valid flights back to the pigeons to group the data by flock name. Determine the average deviation in degrees for each flock, filtering out any flocks where the average deviation is ten degrees or higher. Output the flock name and the average deviation, sorting the results from the smallest deviation to the largest. If the snowy flock deviated by an average of four degrees under strong winds, it would be returned as the first row.

title: Ferret tube racing times
spec: Develop a summary function `measure(length)` that takes a specific tube length as a numeric parameter. You are provided a ferrets table detailing the ferret identifier, name, and coat color. A heats table logs the ferret identifier, tube length in meters, obstacle count, and completion seconds. Extract the race heats that featured more than two obstacles and exactly match the provided tube length. Link these heats to the ferrets table to group the performances by coat color. Find the minimum completion time for each coat color, but only include colors that have logged at least ten valid heats. Return the coat color and the minimum time, ordered from the fastest minimum time to the slowest. For example, given a length of ten meters, the sable coat color might return a minimum time of fifteen seconds.

title: Chameleon color change speeds
spec: Construct a reporting query `quantify(humidity)` that accepts a maximum humidity percentage. A chameleons table tracks the chameleon identifier, habitat region, and current mood. A transitions table records the chameleon identifier, target color, transition time in milliseconds, and humidity percent. Filter the transition logs for events where the target color was red and the humidity was strictly below the provided maximum. Join these logs with the chameleons table to group the occurrences by habitat region. Compute the average transition time in milliseconds for each habitat, keeping only habitats that registered more than fifteen valid color changes. Output the habitat region and the average transition time, sorted from the fastest average time to the slowest. If the desert habitat averaged two hundred milliseconds, it would appear alongside the number two hundred.

title: UFO abduction reports by state
spec: Write a database macro `investigate(minutes)` that accepts a numeric minimum duration. The database contains a witnesses table with the witness identifier, home state, and occupation. An encounters table logs the witness identifier, craft shape, duration in minutes, and a missing time boolean. Narrow the encounters to those where missing time is true and the duration is strictly greater than the given minimum minutes. Merge this data with the witnesses table and group the results by the home state. Count the total number of valid encounters per state, discarding any states that have five or fewer recorded events. Return the home state and the encounter count, sorting the final list from the highest count to the lowest. Example input: a minimum of thirty minutes, which might return the state of Nevada with twelve encounters.

title: Ninja star aerodynamics
spec: Create a query procedure `review(distance)` that takes a numeric minimum throw distance. A shurikens table holds the throwing star identifier, point count, and metal type. A throws table tracks the throwing star identifier, distance traveled in meters, rotation speed, and a boolean indicating if the target was hit. Filter the throws to find only successful target hits where the distance exceeds the provided minimum. Connect these throws to the shurikens table to group the data by point count. Calculate the average rotation speed for each point count, retaining only those groups that have at least twenty successful throws. Output the point count and the average rotation speed, ordering the results from the highest rotation speed to the lowest. A four point star might yield an average rotation speed of three hundred.

title: Bermuda triangle ship disappearances
spec: Write an analytical function `search(days)` that accepts a numeric minimum for days missing. The database features a vessels table logging the ship identifier, ship type, and crew size. A voyages table tracks the ship identifier, cargo type, weather condition, and days missing. Filter the voyage records to isolate trips carrying magnetic cargo where the days missing are strictly greater than the parameter. Join these trips to the vessels table to group the statistics by ship type. Calculate the average crew size for each ship type, restricting the output to ship types with at least three such mysterious voyages. Return the ship type and the average crew size, ordered from the largest average crew to the smallest. A schooner type might be returned with an average crew size of fifteen.

title: Alien crop circle diameters
spec: Develop a geographic query `survey(radiation)` that takes a numeric minimum radiation level. A fields table stores the field identifier, crop type, and country. A circles table records the field identifier, geometry shape, diameter in meters, and radiation level. Filter the crop circle data for those with complex geometry where the radiation level surpasses the provided minimum. Match these circles with the fields table to group the findings by crop type. Determine the maximum diameter for each crop type, keeping only crop types whose average diameter across these filtered events exceeds fifty meters. Output the crop type and the maximum diameter, sorting the rows from the largest maximum diameter to the smallest. For instance, a wheat crop type might output a maximum diameter of one hundred meters.

title: Pirate ship mutiny occurrences
spec: Construct a reporting function `inspect(duration)` that accepts a numeric minimum for mutiny duration in days. A captains table records the captain identifier, name, and a peg leg boolean flag. A mutinies table tracks the captain identifier, ocean location, weapons drawn boolean, and days lasted. Filter the mutiny events to find those where weapons were drawn and the conflict lasted longer than the specified duration. Join these events to the captains table and group the outcomes by the captain name. Count the total number of severe mutinies per captain, retaining only those captains who have faced two or more such events. Output the captain name and the total mutiny count, ordered from the highest count to the lowest. Example: a captain named Blackbeard might be returned with a count of three mutinies.

title: Witch broomstick aerodynamics
spec: Write a performance routine `calibrate(altitude)` that accepts a numeric minimum flight altitude in feet. You have a broomsticks table detailing the broomstick identifier, wood type, and bristle material. A flights table logs the broomstick identifier, altitude in feet, top speed, and a boolean for midnight flights. Filter the flight logs for midnight flights where the altitude was strictly higher than the given minimum. Link these logs with the broomsticks table to group the performances by wood type. Compute the average top speed for each wood type, ensuring you only keep wood types that have at least eight recorded flights in these conditions. Output the wood type and the average top speed, sorting from the highest average speed to the lowest. An ash wood broomstick might output an average top speed of ninety.

title: Werewolf howl decibel tracking
spec: Create a monitoring query `monitor(duration)` that takes a numeric minimum duration in seconds. The database contains a werewolves table with the werewolf identifier, pack name, and fur color. A howls table records the werewolf identifier, moon phase, duration in seconds, and decibel level. Isolate the howling events that occurred during a full moon and lasted longer than the minimum duration. Combine this information with the werewolves table to group the data by pack name. Find the maximum decibel level achieved by each pack, keeping only packs whose average decibel level during these events is above one hundred. Output the pack name and the maximum decibel level, ordered from the loudest maximum decibel to the quietest. The shadow pack might appear in the results with a maximum decibel of one hundred twenty.

title: Space pirate laser battery drain
spec: Develop a diagnostic function `diagnose(cooling)` that accepts a numeric maximum for cooling seconds. A blasters table contains the blaster identifier, model name, and crystal type. A firings table tracks the blaster identifier, target shield type, energy used, and cooling seconds. Filter the firing events to find shots fired at heavy shields where the cooling time was strictly less than the provided maximum. Join these events to the blasters table to group the usage metrics by crystal type. Calculate the average energy used per crystal type, retaining only crystal types that were fired fifty or more times under these constraints. Output the crystal type and the average energy used, sorting the list from the lowest average energy to the highest. A kyber crystal might be listed with an average energy usage of forty.

title: Jovian atmospheric gas harvesting
spec: Write a function called `harvesting(sensors, thresholds)` that evaluates atmospheric resource collection on Jupiter. The first input is a list of tuples containing the sector identifier, gas type, and measured concentration. The second input is a list of tuples containing the gas type and the minimum required concentration for profitable extraction. Return a list of tuples showing the sector identifier and the total number of profitable gases in that sector, but only for sectors that have at least two profitable gases. Sort the final list from highest to lowest number of profitable gases, resolving ties by the sector identifier alphabetically. Example: `harvesting([("Alpha", "Helium", 15), ("Alpha", "Hydrogen", 70)], [("Helium", 20)])` returns `[]`.

title: Trebuchet counterweight physics
spec: Implement `trebuchet(launches, targets)` to analyze medieval siege engine performance. The first parameter is a list of tuples detailing the machine identifier, projectile weight, and distance achieved. The second is a list of tuples with the machine identifier and the distance required to breach the castle walls. Determine which machines successfully breached the walls by throwing a projectile weighing more than fifty kilograms far enough. Return a list of tuples with the machine identifier and the maximum distance it achieved among its successful throws, keeping only machines with a maximum distance exceeding two hundred meters. Order the results by the maximum distance in decreasing order. Example: `trebuchet([("Wolf", 60, 250)], [("Wolf", 200)])` returns `[("Wolf", 250)]`.

title: Submarine sonar acoustic ping mapping
spec: Create a function `sonar(echolocations, vessels)` to map underwater environments. The first argument holds tuples of ping identifier, submarine identifier, and return time in milliseconds. The second argument holds tuples of submarine identifier and maximum operational depth. Calculate the average return time for each submarine that operates deeper than three hundred meters, considering only pings with a return time greater than ten milliseconds. Return tuples of the submarine identifier and its average return time, restricted to submarines whose average is below fifty milliseconds. Sort the output alphabetically by the submarine identifier. Example: `sonar([("P1", "Nautilus", 15)], [("Nautilus", 400)])` returns `[("Nautilus", 15.0)]`.

title: Quantum entanglement teleportation logs
spec: Write `entanglement(particles, stations)` to track subatomic teleportation. The first list contains tuples of particle identifier, station identifier, and spin state stability score. The second list contains tuples of station identifier and target destination coordinates. Find the destinations that received particles with a stability score above ninety. Group the results by the destination coordinates and calculate the total number of stable particles received. Return tuples of the destination and the particle count, filtering out destinations that received fewer than five stable particles. Order the results by the particle count from lowest to highest. Example: `entanglement([("Q1", "S1", 95)], [("S1", "MarsBase")])` returns `[]`.

title: Giant squid ink gland capacity
spec: Develop `squid(specimens, oceans)` to evaluate marine biology metrics. The first list provides tuples of researcher name, ocean region, and liters of ink extracted. The second list provides tuples of ocean region and the baseline expected ink volume in liters. Identify researchers who extracted more than the baseline volume for their specific region. For these successful extractions, compute the total excess volume for each region. Return tuples of the ocean region and the sum of the excess volumes, including only regions where the sum exceeds twenty liters. Sort the output by the ocean region alphabetically. Example: `squid([("Nemo", "Pacific", 120)], [("Pacific", 90)])` returns `[("Pacific", 30)]`.

title: Steampunk brass gear fabrication
spec: Formulate `brass(gears, blueprints)` to monitor Victorian mechanical part production. The first input comprises tuples of batch identifier, blueprint name, and the measured diameter of the produced gear. The second input comprises tuples of blueprint name, target diameter, and acceptable tolerance. Filter the gears to find those that fall strictly outside the acceptable tolerance range for their blueprint. Group the defective gears by blueprint name and count the number of defects. Output a list of tuples containing the blueprint name and the defect count, keeping only blueprints with at least three defects. Sort the list descending by the defect count. Example: `brass([("B1", "CogA", 10.5)], [("CogA", 10.0, 0.2)])` returns `[]`.

title: Dwarven anvil strike resonance
spec: Build `anvil(strikes, metals)` to investigate subterranean metallurgy techniques. The first argument is a list of tuples containing the strike identifier, metal type, and acoustic resonance frequency in hertz. The second argument is a list of tuples containing the metal type and target forging frequency. Select strikes where the target forging frequency is above four hundred hertz and the recorded acoustic resonance differs by more than fifty hertz from the target. Compute the average resonance frequency for each metal type from these aberrant strikes. Return tuples of the metal type and the average frequency, but only for metals that have more than two aberrant strikes. Order the final list by the average frequency in ascending order. Example: `anvil([("S1", "Mithril", 500)], [("Mithril", 400)])` returns `[]`.

title: Interstellar comet ice mining
spec: Code `comet(extractions, ships)` to manage deep space water resources. The first collection holds tuples of extraction identifier, ship name, and cubic meters of ice mined. The second collection holds tuples of ship name and cargo capacity in cubic meters. Determine which extractions exceed ten percent of the ship's total cargo capacity. For each ship, sum the volume of these massive extractions. Produce a list of tuples with the ship name and the total massive extraction volume, filtering out ships whose total is less than five hundred cubic meters. Sort the records alphabetically by ship name. Example: `comet([("E1", "Voyager", 60)], [("Voyager", 500)])` returns `[]`.

title: Manticore tail spike ballistics
spec: Implement `manticore(spikes, armors)` to study mythical beast combat mechanics. The first parameter is a list of tuples containing the spike identifier, armor type struck, and penetration depth recorded. The second parameter is a list of tuples containing the armor type and the minimum penetration depth required to inflict injury. Find the spikes that achieved a penetration depth greater than the minimum required for the armor type they hit. Count the number of successful penetrations for each armor type. Return tuples of the armor type and the count, restricted to armor types with at least ten successful penetrations. Order the output by armor type descending. Example: `manticore([("S1", "Steel", 20)], [("Steel", 15)])` returns `[]`.

title: Carnivorous plant digestion rates
spec: Write `digestion(plants, insects)` to analyze botanical feeding habits. The first list of tuples contains the plant species, the insect type consumed, and the digestion time in hours. The second list of tuples contains the insect type and its exoskeleton thickness rating. Filter for digestion events where the exoskeleton thickness is rated higher than seven and the digestion time is under forty eight hours. Group the remaining records by plant species and calculate the average digestion time. Yield tuples of the plant species and the average time, excluding species whose average time is above thirty hours. Sort alphabetically by plant species. Example: `digestion([("Flytrap", "Beetle", 24)], [("Beetle", 8)])` returns `[("Flytrap", 24.0)]`.

title: Mechanical music box cylinder pinning
spec: Create `cylinder(pins, melodies)` to evaluate antique audio reproduction. The first argument represents tuples of cylinder identifier, melody name, and the count of missing pins. The second argument represents tuples of melody name and the total original pin count. Calculate the missing pin percentage for each cylinder by joining the lists on the melody name. Select cylinders where the missing pin percentage is below five percent. Group by the melody name to find the maximum missing pin count among these well preserved cylinders. Output tuples of the melody name and this maximum count, but only if the melody has more than one well preserved cylinder. Order the results by the maximum count ascending. Example: `cylinder([("C1", "FurElise", 2)], [("FurElise", 100)])` returns `[]`.

title: Foghorn acoustic range testing
spec: Write `foghorn(tests, locations)` to verify maritime warning systems. The first input contains tuples of test identifier, location name, and the maximum audible distance in kilometers. The second input contains tuples of location name and the historical average audible distance. Identify tests where the maximum audible distance is at least two kilometers greater than the historical average. For each location, count the number of these superior tests. Return a list of tuples with the location name and the count, keeping only locations with exactly three superior tests. Sort the records alphabetically by location name. Example: `foghorn([("T1", "Bay", 15)], [("Bay", 12)])` returns `[]`.

title: Deep sea habitat pressure window testing
spec: Develop `habitat(windows, materials)` to ensure structural integrity of underwater observation outposts. The first sequence holds tuples of window identifier, material name, and the detected microfracture count after pressurization. The second sequence holds tuples of material name and its tensile strength rating. Filter the windows to only include those made of a material with a tensile strength rating of fifty or higher, and which possess fewer than five microfractures. Group by the material name and compute the total number of windows that passed. Return tuples of the material name and the passed window count, limiting to materials that had more than twenty windows pass. Order the output descending by the passed window count. Example: `habitat([("W1", "Acrylic", 2)], [("Acrylic", 60)])` returns `[]`.

title: Church bell bronze casting
spec: Build `bronze(bells, foundries)` to track artisanal metalwork. The first parameter provides tuples of bell identifier, foundry name, and the cooling duration in days. The second parameter provides tuples of foundry name and the ambient humidity percentage during the season. Focus on bells cast at foundries with an ambient humidity below forty percent that took longer than ten days to cool. For each foundry, determine the average cooling duration of these specific bells. Output tuples of the foundry name and the average duration, excluding foundries where the average is less than fourteen days. Sort the list alphabetically by foundry name. Example: `bronze([("B1", "Ironworks", 15)], [("Ironworks", 30)])` returns `[("Ironworks", 15.0)]`.

title: Pop up book paper engineering
spec: Formulate `popup(pages, mechanisms)` to assess interactive literature durability. The first list contains tuples of book title, mechanism type, and the number of folds before tearing. The second list contains tuples of mechanism type and the paper weight in grams per square meter. Select testing records where the paper weight exceeds two hundred grams and the folds before tearing are fewer than fifty. Group the results by book title and count the number of fragile mechanisms. Return tuples of the book title and the fragile mechanism count, showing only books with more than four fragile mechanisms. Order by the count descending. Example: `popup([("Castle", "V-Fold", 30)], [("V-Fold", 250)])` returns `[]`.

title: Animatronic dinosaur joint lubrication
spec: Code `animatronic(joints, fluids)` to maintain theme park attractions. The first argument consists of tuples containing the dinosaur identifier, fluid brand, and the friction coefficient measured. The second argument consists of tuples containing the fluid brand and its viscosity index. Join the data to find joints using a fluid with a viscosity index over one hundred that still exhibit a friction coefficient above zero point five. Group by the dinosaur identifier to sum the total friction of these problematic joints. Yield tuples of the dinosaur identifier and the total friction, dropping dinosaurs with a total friction below two. Sort the results alphabetically by dinosaur identifier. Example: `animatronic([("Rex", "LubeX", 0.6)], [("LubeX", 120)])` returns `[]`.

title: Bungee jump cord tension limits
spec: Implement `bungee(jumps, cords)` to guarantee extreme sports safety. The first input provides tuples of jump identifier, cord identifier, and the maximum extension length in meters. The second input provides tuples of cord identifier and the theoretical elastic limit in meters. Identify jumps where the extension length exceeded ninety five percent of the theoretical elastic limit. For each cord, count how many such extreme jumps occurred. Return a list of tuples containing the cord identifier and the extreme jump count, including only cords with at least two extreme jumps. Order the final output descending by the count. Example: `bungee([("J1", "C1", 96), ("J2", "C1", 97)], [("C1", 100)])` returns `[("C1", 2)]`.

title: Orbital satellite thruster fuel consumption
spec: Write `thruster(burns, engines)` to monitor extraterrestrial vehicle health. The first list of tuples contains the burn identifier, engine model, and the recorded fuel expenditure in kilograms. The second list of tuples contains the engine model and the maximum efficient fuel expenditure limit. Filter for burns where the recorded expenditure is strictly greater than the maximum efficient limit. Group the inefficient burns by engine model and find the highest recorded expenditure for each. Produce tuples of the engine model and this peak expenditure, keeping only models whose peak expenditure exceeds fifty kilograms. Sort the list alphabetically by engine model. Example: `thruster([("B1", "IonX", 55)], [("IonX", 40)])` returns `[("IonX", 55)]`.

title: Camel caravan water rationing
spec: Create `caravan(stops, camels)` to optimize desert travel logistics. The first parameter contains tuples of stop name, camel identifier, and the liters of water consumed. The second parameter contains tuples of camel identifier and their humps count. Focus on records of camels with exactly two humps that consumed more than twenty liters of water at a single stop. Group the filtered data by the stop name and calculate the total water consumed by these camels. Output tuples of the stop name and the total water consumed, omitting stops where the total is under one hundred liters. Order the results descending by the total water consumed. Example: `caravan([("Oasis", "C1", 25)], [("C1", 2)])` returns `[]`.

title: Deep earth magma chamber mapping
spec: Write a function `magma(sensors, strata)` to analyze geological activity. The first input is a list of tuples containing the sensor identifier, rock layer name, and the detected temperature in celsius. The second input is a list of tuples containing the rock layer name and its melting point. Select sensor readings where the detected temperature is within fifty degrees of the melting point. Group the data by the rock layer name and count the number of critical temperature readings. Return tuples of the rock layer name and the critical reading count, restricted to layers with more than ten critical readings. Sort the output alphabetically by the rock layer name. Example: `magma([("S1", "Basalt", 1150)], [("Basalt", 1200)])` returns `[]`.

title: Android empathy chip testing
spec: Develop `empathy(responses, scenarios)` to evaluate artificial emotional intelligence. The first argument holds tuples of android identifier, scenario name, and the measured empathy score from one to ten. The second argument holds tuples of scenario name and the baseline human empathy score. Find responses where the android scored at least two points lower than the human baseline. Group the deficient responses by the android identifier and calculate their average empathy score in these failed scenarios. Yield tuples of the android identifier and the average score, but only for androids that failed more than five scenarios. Order the list by the average score ascending. Example: `empathy([("A1", "SadMovie", 4)], [("SadMovie", 8)])` returns `[]`.

title: Hoverboard anti gravity coil cooling
spec: Code `hoverboard(coils, coolants)` to prevent futuristic urban transport fires. The first sequence provides tuples of coil identifier, coolant brand, and the operating temperature in kelvin. The second sequence provides tuples of coolant brand and its boiling point in kelvin. Identify coils where the operating temperature surpasses the boiling point of their respective coolant. For each coolant brand, count the number of overheating coils. Return a list of tuples with the coolant brand and the overheating coil count, keeping only brands associated with exactly zero safe coils, which for simplicity means filtering for counts greater than twenty. Sort the records descending by the count. Example: `hoverboard([("C1", "CryoX", 350)], [("CryoX", 300)])` returns `[]`.

title: Warp drive plasma containment
spec: Build `plasma(leaks, shields)` to ensure temporal travel safety. The first collection consists of tuples containing the jump identifier, shield model, and the leaked plasma volume. The second collection consists of tuples containing the shield model and the maximum absorption capacity. Filter the leaks to isolate jumps where the leaked plasma exceeds the maximum absorption capacity of the used shield. Group these dangerous jumps by the shield model and sum the total leaked volume. Output tuples of the shield model and the total leak volume, filtering out models with a total leak volume below ten thousand units. Order the results alphabetically by the shield model. Example: `plasma([("J1", "Aegis", 12000)], [("Aegis", 10000)])` returns `[("Aegis", 12000)]`.

title: Ogre cave stalactite hazards
spec: Implement `stalactite(caves, ogres)` to assess monster dwelling safety. The first list of tuples contains the cave identifier, ogre clan name, and the number of falling stalactites per month. The second list of tuples contains the ogre clan name and their average helmet thickness in millimeters. Find caves inhabited by clans with an average helmet thickness below ten millimeters that experience more than five falling stalactites a month. Group the hazardous caves by the clan name and compute the maximum number of falling stalactites recorded in a single cave. Return tuples of the clan name and the maximum stalactite count, restricted to counts above fifteen. Sort the output descending by the maximum count. Example: `stalactite([("SkullCave", "Bonecrusher", 20)], [("Bonecrusher", 8)])` returns `[("Bonecrusher", 20)]`.

title: Alchemy lead to gold transmutation impurities
spec: Formulate `alchemy(batches, catalysts)` to perfect ancient mystical chemistry. The first parameter provides tuples of batch identifier, catalyst name, and the percentage of lead remaining. The second parameter provides tuples of catalyst name and its purity rating out of one hundred. Select transmutation batches where the catalyst purity rating is below ninety and the remaining lead percentage is greater than five. Group by the catalyst name and average the remaining lead percentage across the failed batches. Yield tuples of the catalyst name and the average lead percentage, omitting catalysts that were used in fewer than three failed batches. Order the results descending by the average lead percentage. Example: `alchemy([("B1", "DragonBlood", 10)], [("DragonBlood", 85)])` returns `[]`.

title: Interstellar jump gate coordinate misalignments
spec: Write a SQL-backed function named `align(gates, jumps)`. The gates data includes a gate identifier, a sector name, and a base stability score. The jumps data tracks a jump identifier, the gate identifier, a misalignment angle, and a jump year. Join the two datasets to calculate the average misalignment angle for each sector name. Only consider jumps that occurred after the year three thousand, and only include gates that have a base stability score below fifty. Group the results by sector name and filter to keep only those sectors where the average misalignment angle is strictly greater than ten. Return a list of tuples containing the sector name and the average misalignment angle, ordered by the angle in descending order. Example input: gates with sector Orion and stability forty, jumps with angles twelve and sixteen. Example output: [("Orion", 14)].

title: Hover car traffic violation citations
spec: Write a SQL-powered function named `patrol(vehicles, citations)`. The vehicles dataset has a vehicle identifier, an owner name, and a propulsion type. The citations dataset has a citation identifier, the vehicle identifier, a violation speed, and a penalty fee. Join the datasets to calculate the total penalty fees accumulated by each owner. Filter the records to only include vehicles that use magnetic propulsion and violations where the speed exceeded one hundred. Group the data by owner name and only retain owners whose total penalty fees are greater than three hundred. Return a list of tuples with the owner name and their total fee, sorted from highest total fee to lowest. Example input: vehicles with owner Zara and magnetic propulsion, citations with two fees of two hundred. Example output: [("Zara", 400)].

title: Underwater dome city structural microfractures
spec: Write a function using SQL named `inspect(sectors, fractures)`. The sectors list contains a sector identifier, a zone name, and a depth level. The fractures list includes a fracture identifier, the sector identifier, a crack length, and a water pressure reading. Join the two lists to determine the average crack length for each zone name. Filter the data to only include sectors at a depth level greater than two thousand and fractures where the water pressure was above normal levels. Group by the zone name and keep only the zones where the average crack length exceeds five millimeters. Return a list of tuples with the zone name and the average length, sorted by the average length in descending order. Example input: sectors with zone Abyssal and depth three thousand, fractures with lengths six and eight at high pressure. Example output: [("Abyssal", 7)].

title: Nanobot blood cell repair efficiency
spec: Create a SQL-based function named `evaluate(patients, repairs)`. The patients dataset provides a patient identifier, a blood type, and a nanobot model. The repairs dataset logs a repair identifier, the patient identifier, the number of cells repaired, and the duration in minutes. Join the datasets to find the total number of cells repaired by each nanobot model. Filter the analysis to only include patients with type O positive blood and repairs that took longer than thirty minutes. Group the results by nanobot model and retain only models that repaired more than ten thousand cells in total. Return a list of tuples containing the nanobot model and the total cells repaired, ordered by the total cells from highest to lowest. Example input: patients with model Alpha and type O positive, repairs with six thousand and five thousand cells. Example output: [("Alpha", 11000)].

title: Gravity plating failure anomalies on starships
spec: Write a SQL-driven function named `calibrate(decks, anomalies)`. The decks input features a deck identifier, a ship name, and a deck type. The anomalies input contains an anomaly identifier, the deck identifier, a gravity drop percentage, and a duration in seconds. Join the two datasets to sum the total duration of gravity anomalies for each ship name. Limit the data to passenger deck types and anomalies where the gravity drop percentage was greater than twenty. Group by the ship name and filter for ships where the total anomaly duration exceeds three hundred seconds. Return a list of tuples with the ship name and the total duration, sorted by the total duration descending. Example input: decks with ship Voyager and passenger type, anomalies with durations of two hundred and one hundred fifty. Example output: [("Voyager", 350)].

title: Biodome artificial sunlight spectrum variations
spec: Write a SQL-backed function named `monitor(panels, readings)`. The panels data has a panel identifier, a biome type, and an installation year. The readings data contains a reading identifier, the panel identifier, a spectrum shift value, and an intensity level. Join these records to compute the average spectrum shift for each biome type. Include only panels installed before the year two thousand and fifty, and readings where the intensity level was below eighty. Group the results by biome type and filter to include only biomes with an average spectrum shift greater than four. Return a list of tuples containing the biome type and average shift, ordered by the shift in descending order. Example input: panels in the tropical biome installed in two thousand, readings with shifts of five and seven. Example output: [("tropical", 6)].

title: Teleportation pad molecular scattering incidents
spec: Create a function utilizing SQL named `audit(pads, incidents)`. The pads table holds a pad identifier, a station name, and a calibration frequency in days. The incidents table tracks an incident identifier, the pad identifier, a scattered mass in grams, and a recovery time. Join the tables to calculate the total scattered mass for each station name. Filter the records for pads that have a calibration frequency greater than thirty days and incidents with a recovery time over five minutes. Group by the station name and keep only stations with a total scattered mass exceeding fifty grams. Return a list of tuples containing the station name and total mass, ordered by mass descending. Example input: pads at station Delta with sixty days frequency, incidents with thirty and forty grams. Example output: [("Delta", 70)].

title: Cryogenic stasis pod thaw sequence errors
spec: Write a SQL-based function named `defrost(pods, logs)`. The pods list contains a pod identifier, a vessel name, and a coolant type. The logs list features a log identifier, the pod identifier, a temperature spike in degrees, and an error code. Join the datasets to find the maximum temperature spike for each vessel name. Only consider pods that use liquid helium as their coolant type and logs where the error code is not zero. Group by the vessel name and filter for vessels where the maximum temperature spike is greater than three degrees. Return a list of tuples with the vessel name and the maximum spike, sorted by the spike value from highest to lowest. Example input: pods on vessel Aurora using liquid helium, logs with spikes of two and five. Example output: [("Aurora", 5)].

title: Mech suit armor plating ablation tracking
spec: Implement a SQL-powered function named `armor(suits, battles)`. The suits input provides a suit identifier, a pilot name, and a chassis class. The battles input tracks a battle identifier, the suit identifier, an ablation depth in millimeters, and the number of hits taken. Join the datasets to determine the total ablation depth per pilot name. Restrict the data to heavy chassis class suits and battles where the hits taken were greater than twenty. Group by the pilot name and only include pilots whose total ablation depth is over one hundred millimeters. Return a list of tuples with the pilot name and total ablation depth, sorted by depth descending. Example input: suits piloted by Jax in a heavy chassis, battles with depths of sixty and fifty. Example output: [("Jax", 110)].

title: Xenobiology tissue sample mutation rates
spec: Write a SQL-driven function named `mutate(samples, observations)`. The samples dataset has a sample identifier, a species name, and a containment level. The observations dataset logs an observation identifier, the sample identifier, a mutation percentage, and a radiation dose. Join the records to calculate the average mutation percentage for each species name. Filter for samples at the maximum containment level and observations where the radiation dose exceeded five hundred units. Group by species name and retain only species with an average mutation percentage above fifteen. Return a list of tuples containing the species name and average mutation, ordered by mutation descending. Example input: samples of species Xenomorph at maximum containment, observations with percentages of ten and twenty. Example output: [("Xenomorph", 15)].

title: Deep space relay comms packet loss
spec: Create a function using SQL named `transmit(relays, packets)`. The relays data includes a relay identifier, a quadrant name, and an antenna type. The packets data contains a packet identifier, the relay identifier, the number of packets lost, and a latency in milliseconds. Join the datasets to calculate the total packets lost for each quadrant name. Consider only relays with a dish antenna type and packet records where the latency was over two thousand milliseconds. Group by the quadrant name and filter for quadrants with total packets lost exceeding one million. Return a list of tuples containing the quadrant name and total packets lost, sorted descending by packets lost. Example input: relays in the Alpha quadrant with dish antennas, packet records showing six hundred thousand and five hundred thousand lost. Example output: [("Alpha", 1100000)].

title: Plasma rifle coolant cartridge depletion
spec: Write a SQL-backed function named `reload(rifles, usages)`. The rifles table lists a rifle identifier, a squad name, and a battery capacity. The usages table tracks a usage identifier, the rifle identifier, a coolant drained percentage, and the number of shots fired. Join the tables to compute the average coolant drained for each squad name. Filter the data to include only rifles with a battery capacity over five hundred and usages where more than fifty shots were fired. Group by squad name and keep only those squads where the average coolant drained is strictly above eighty percent. Return a list of tuples with the squad name and average drain, ordered from highest drain to lowest. Example input: rifles for squad Bravo with capacity six hundred, usages draining eighty and ninety percent. Example output: [("Bravo", 85)].

title: Hologram billboard light emitter failures
spec: Write a SQL-powered function named `broadcast(billboards, glitches)`. The billboards input provides a billboard identifier, a district name, and a display resolution. The glitches input contains a glitch identifier, the billboard identifier, a count of dead pixels, and a downtime in minutes. Join the datasets to find the total dead pixels for each district name. Only include billboards with an ultra high display resolution and glitches where the downtime was greater than ten minutes. Group by district name and retain only districts that have accumulated over five hundred dead pixels in total. Return a list of tuples containing the district name and total dead pixels, sorted by dead pixels descending. Example input: billboards in the Neon district with ultra high resolution, glitches with three hundred and two hundred fifty dead pixels. Example output: [("Neon", 550)].

title: Sub-orbital flight passenger zero gravity nausea
spec: Create a SQL-based function named `fly(flights, passengers)`. The flights list has a flight identifier, a pilot name, and an apogee altitude in kilometers. The passengers list logs a passenger identifier, the flight identifier, a nausea severity score, and a medication administered flag. Join the lists to calculate the average nausea severity score for each pilot name. Filter the data to only include flights with an apogee altitude over one hundred kilometers and passengers who did not have medication administered. Group by pilot name and keep only pilots whose flights average a nausea severity greater than seven. Return a list of tuples containing the pilot name and average severity, ordered by severity descending. Example input: flights by pilot Riker reaching one hundred twenty kilometers, passengers with unmedicated nausea scores of eight and ten. Example output: [("Riker", 9)].

title: Antimatter reactor containment field fluctuations
spec: Write a function utilizing SQL named `contain(reactors, fluctuations)`. The reactors dataset contains a reactor identifier, a facility name, and a core age in years. The fluctuations dataset tracks a fluctuation identifier, the reactor identifier, a variance percentage, and a magnetic field strength. Join the datasets to determine the maximum variance percentage for each facility name. Restrict the data to reactors with a core age greater than ten years and fluctuations where the magnetic field strength was below fifty units. Group by facility name and only include facilities where the maximum variance percentage is above five. Return a list of tuples with the facility name and maximum variance, sorted by variance descending. Example input: reactors at facility Prime aged twelve years, fluctuations with variances of four and seven. Example output: [("Prime", 7)].

title: Cyberware optic lens calibration drift
spec: Implement a SQL-driven function named `focus(implants, scans)`. The implants table provides an implant identifier, a manufacturer name, and a firmware version. The scans table includes a scan identifier, the implant identifier, a drift angle, and a visual artifact count. Join the tables to find the average visual artifact count for each manufacturer name. Filter for implants running firmware version two and scans where the drift angle was greater than one degree. Group by manufacturer name and filter to keep only manufacturers with an average artifact count greater than three. Return a list of tuples containing the manufacturer name and average artifact count, ordered by the count in descending order. Example input: implants by manufacturer Kiroshi on version two, scans with artifact counts of three and five. Example output: [("Kiroshi", 4)].

title: Dyson sphere solar panel alignment errors
spec: Write a SQL-backed function named `adjust(sectors, alignments)`. The sectors input features a sector identifier, a latitude ring, and a panel count. The alignments input logs an alignment identifier, the sector identifier, a deviation in degrees, and an energy loss value. Join the datasets to calculate the total energy loss for each latitude ring. Include only sectors that have a panel count above one thousand and alignments where the deviation was greater than two degrees. Group the results by latitude ring and retain only rings where the total energy loss exceeds ten thousand units. Return a list of tuples with the latitude ring and total energy loss, sorted by energy loss descending. Example input: sectors in the Equatorial ring with two thousand panels, alignments showing energy losses of six thousand and five thousand. Example output: [("Equatorial", 11000)].

title: Orbital elevator counterweight vibrational stress
spec: Create a SQL-powered function named `balance(tethers, vibrations)`. The tethers dataset includes a tether identifier, a material type, and a load capacity in tons. The vibrations dataset tracks a vibration identifier, the tether identifier, a frequency in hertz, and an amplitude in millimeters. Join the datasets to compute the average vibration amplitude for each material type. Filter the records for tethers with a load capacity over fifty tons and vibrations where the frequency was below twenty hertz. Group by material type and only include materials with an average vibration amplitude greater than fifteen millimeters. Return a list of tuples containing the material type and average amplitude, sorted descending by amplitude. Example input: tethers made of carbon nanotubes with sixty tons capacity, vibrations with amplitudes of fourteen and eighteen. Example output: [("carbon nanotubes", 16)].

title: Lunar mining railgun payload trajectories
spec: Write a SQL-based function named `launch(railguns, payloads)`. The railguns table has a railgun identifier, a crater name, and a barrel length in meters. The payloads table contains a payload identifier, the railgun identifier, a launch velocity, and an off course distance in meters. Join the tables to find the average off course distance for each crater name. Filter the data to include only railguns with a barrel length over five hundred meters and payloads with a launch velocity exceeding eleven kilometers per second. Group by crater name and keep only those craters where the average off course distance is over fifty meters. Return a list of tuples with the crater name and average distance, ordered descending by distance. Example input: railguns in the Tycho crater with six hundred meter barrels, payloads off course by forty and seventy meters. Example output: [("Tycho", 55)].

title: Bio-engineered coral reef calcium absorption
spec: Write a function using SQL named `grow(reefs, measurements)`. The reefs data lists a reef identifier, an ocean region, and a coral strain. The measurements data tracks a measurement identifier, the reef identifier, a calcium uptake value, and a water acidity level. Join the lists to sum the total calcium uptake for each ocean region. Consider only reefs growing the luminescent coral strain and measurements where the water acidity level was above eight. Group by ocean region and filter for regions where the total calcium uptake exceeds one thousand units. Return a list of tuples containing the ocean region and total calcium uptake, sorted by uptake in descending order. Example input: reefs in the Pacific region with luminescent strain, measurements showing uptakes of six hundred and five hundred. Example output: [("Pacific", 1100)].

title: Asteroid base atmospheric scrubber efficiency
spec: Implement a SQL-driven function named `scrub(bases, cycles)`. The bases input provides a base identifier, an asteroid name, and a population count. The cycles input contains a cycle identifier, the base identifier, a carbon dioxide removed amount, and a filter status. Join the datasets to calculate the average carbon dioxide removed for each asteroid name. Filter the records to include only bases with a population count over five hundred and cycles where the filter status is marked as dirty. Group by asteroid name and retain only asteroids where the average carbon dioxide removed is below fifty units. Return a list of tuples with the asteroid name and average removal amount, ordered ascending by the removal amount. Example input: bases on asteroid Ceres with six hundred people, cycles removing forty and forty eight units on dirty filters. Example output: [("Ceres", 44)].

title: Sentient AI processing core thermal throttling
spec: Write a SQL-backed function named `cool(cores, temperatures)`. The cores table features a core identifier, an artificial intelligence name, and an architecture type. The temperatures table logs a temperature identifier, the core identifier, a heat level, and a throttle duration in seconds. Join the tables to find the total throttle duration for each artificial intelligence name. Restrict the data to cores using a quantum architecture type and temperature records where the heat level exceeded ninety degrees. Group by artificial intelligence name and filter for those with a total throttle duration over two hundred seconds. Return a list of tuples containing the artificial intelligence name and total duration, sorted by duration descending. Example input: cores for artificial intelligence Hal with quantum architecture, temperatures with throttle durations of one hundred and one hundred fifty seconds. Example output: [("Hal", 250)].

title: Martian dust storm rover navigation delays
spec: Create a SQL-powered function named `navigate(rovers, routes)`. The rovers dataset contains a rover identifier, a rover model, and a solar efficiency percentage. The routes dataset includes a route identifier, the rover identifier, a dust opacity level, and a delay in minutes. Join the datasets to compute the average delay for each rover model. Filter the data to include only rovers with a solar efficiency percentage below sixty and routes where the dust opacity level was greater than seven. Group by rover model and keep only those models where the average delay exceeds thirty minutes. Return a list of tuples with the rover model and average delay, ordered descending by average delay. Example input: rovers of model Explorer with fifty percent efficiency, routes delayed by twenty and forty-four minutes. Example output: [("Explorer", 32)].

title: Warp drive plasma coil resonance cascading
spec: Write a SQL-based function named `warp(drives, pulses)`. The drives list provides a drive identifier, a starship class, and a coil composition.
